Header: Setosphaeria turcica Turcicum leaf blight, Northern leaf blight

Prevention: To reduce initial inoculum, use tillage methods that promote the decomposition of crop debris, as the fungus survives in and on plant debris.
Practise crop rotation with non-grass crops and eliminate weedy grass hosts.
On sorghum, increased levels of nitrogen increase the development of the disease.
Avoid high levels of nitrogen fertilization.
Crop rotation for 1-2 years with soybeans, beans and sunflower.
Do not practise crop rotation with maize.
Monitoring: Monitor regularly for symptoms during optimal conditions of high humidity and moderate temperatures (18-27 °C).
Initially slightly oval, small, water-soaked spots appear.
The spots grow into elliptical (with pointed ends) brown lesions until nearly as wide as the leaf.
The margin is red-purple and during warm, humid weather, greenish-black fungal sporulation is produced in the centre of the lesions.
In the final stages, lesions are tan to grey, may merge and lead to complete burning of the foliage.
Lesions develop first on lower leaves and progress upwards.
Seedlings: small reddish-purple or yellowish-brown spots usually develop on the leaves.
Under warm, humid conditions the disease may cause serious damage by killing all leaves before plants have matured.
Symptoms on resistant cultivars are reduced to small chlorotic or necrotic spots.
S. turcica on sorghum forms larger and fewer lesions than
Cochliobolus heterostrophus (southern leaf spot), mostly on the leaves but also on the stalks.
Cercospora , Colletorichum , Ascochyta can also cause similar leaf disease symptoms.
Act when the first lesions appear on the leaves.
Direct Control (Non-chemical): There are no direct control measures for this disease.
